name: dedupe
maintainer: dedupe.io / Forest Gregg and Derek Eder
purpose: Python library for fuzzy deduplication and record linkage that uses active learning: it asks a human to label borderline pairs, learns blocking predicates and comparison weights, then clusters records.
journalism_use_case: The classic newsroom tool for collapsing duplicate rows in a messy registry, donor list or permit database. The active-learning console is the point: a reporter who knows the domain supplies the match/no-match judgements, so the resolution encodes editorial knowledge rather than an engineer's guess.
pros: Active learning puts the domain expert in the loop, which is the right division of labour for newsroom data and produces defensible clusters
Long lineage in civic-tech and data journalism; the CSV wrappers (csvdedupe) let an analyst work without writing code
Learns blocking predicates automatically, removing the hardest part of naive record linkage
MIT, local, no infrastructure
cons: No tagged release since v3.0.3 and the repository has not been pushed since 2025-07-29 — the clearest maintenance warning in this subcategory
Does not scale comfortably past a few million records; memory and training time become the binding constraint where Splink would not
Results depend on the labelling session, so two reporters can produce different clusters from the same data — reproducibility requires saving and version-controlling the training file
Documentation assumes statistical familiarity; the m/u and blocking concepts are not explained in reporter-friendly terms
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The documented signal is negative and checkable: last push 2025-07-29 with no release since v3.0.3 against 4,530 stars and 93 open issues — a widely used library whose maintenance has visibly slowed. The commercial dedupe.io hosted service is a separate product from this library and its continued operation does not evidence library maintenance.
assessment: I would not start a new project on dedupe in 2026. Splink does the same job with better scaling, active maintenance and auditable match weights, and is the honest recommendation for your profile. Keep dedupe in the catalogue because existing newsroom pipelines use it and because the active-learning UX is still the most reporter-friendly way to resolve a small, messy list — but treat it as a tool with a succession plan.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2025-07-29 (over 15 months stale), no GitHub release object, latest tag 'wide_windows_build', 4,530 stars, 93 open issues. Classified declining rather than dormant because the project is a finished library in wide use and no deprecation notice exists; but the absence of both commits and releases for over a year against an open issue backlog is substantive evidence, not a quiet-mature pattern.
licence_restrictions: None. Note the hosted dedupe.io service is a separate commercial product under its own terms — the MIT licence covers only this library.
costs: Library free. The hosted dedupe.io service is priced separately and was not verified in this survey (not publicly confirmed here). Operating cost is analyst labelling time — typically an hour or two per dataset — plus CPU.
privacy: Fully local; the library makes no network calls. Do not confuse it with the hosted dedupe.io service, which would involve uploading your data to a third party.
alternatives: Splink — recommended replacement: scales further, actively maintained, auditable match weights
RapidFuzz plus manual blocking for small one-off jobs
nomenklatura if your data is already mapped to FollowTheMoney
blockers: No commits or releases since July 2025 — unsuitable as a new long-term dependency
summary: Python library for fuzzy deduplication and record linkage that uses active learning: it asks a human to label borderline pairs…

name: Docling
maintainer: docling-project (IBM Research origin, now LF AI & Data)
purpose: Document conversion library that parses PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, HTML and images into a unified DoclingDocument model with layout, reading order and table structure, exporting to Markdown, JSON and HTML.
journalism_use_case: Permissively licensed, fully local parsing for sensitive leaks where even model-weight restrictions are unacceptable — the key differentiator against Marker/Surya. The unified document model with page provenance means you can cite 'page 14, table 2' back to the original, which matters when an extraction becomes evidence.
pros: MIT code with layout and TableFormer models published by the project itself — the only strong layout-aware parser in this catalogue without an OpenRAIL-M or revenue-threshold condition
Unified DoclingDocument model preserves reading order, table structure and page provenance, which is what makes repeatable newsroom ingest possible
Backed by LF AI & Data with a very high release cadence (v2.150.1, 2026-11-14) and 70,691 stars — exceptional institutional and community momentum
Pluggable OCR backends (Tesseract, EasyOCR, RapidOCR) and optional VLM pipelines, so you can trade accuracy for speed per corpus
cons: The release cadence is itself a cost: API churn across 2.x point releases means pinning is mandatory and upgrades need regression tests on your own documents
OCR quality is entirely the plugged-in backend's — Docling does not fix Tesseract's weakness on degraded scans

Model licences were not individually verified in this survey: layout and TableFormer weights are distributed via HuggingFace under the docling-project org and per-model terms remain unconfirmed, so the 'fully permissive' claim is strong for code and probable but unverified for weights
1,071 open issues; at this growth rate support is diluted and you should expect to read source
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The quantitative signals are strong and checkable: 70,691 stars and a release on 2026-11-14 indicate rapid adoption. The 1,071 open issues are documented evidence of support strain. No journalism-specific deployment verified.
assessment: My recommended default parser for sensitive material, specifically because it sidesteps the weights-licence problem that makes Marker and Surya awkward for a commercially operated newsroom. Two conditions: pin the version, and verify the specific model weights you download rather than inheriting my 'probable' assessment. If you need maximum accuracy on messy multi-column scans and your revenue is under Datalab's threshold, Marker may still beat it — evaluate both on your own documents.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v2.150.1 (2026-11-14), 70,691 stars, 1,071 open issues. Release-per-week cadence plus LF AI & Data governance; the maintenance question here is churn, not neglect.
model_or_data_licence: NOT individually verified. Layout and TableFormer models are distributed via HuggingFace under the docling-project organisation; per-model terms unconfirmed as of 2026-11-17.
licence_restrictions: Code is unrestricted. Residual uncertainty at the weights layer — confirm the licence of each model you pull before relying on it for commercial publication.
costs: No fee. CPU-viable for born-digital documents; a GPU materially helps the VLM pipelines and large scanned batches. First run downloads models from HuggingFace (one-off egress; can be pre-staged). Infrastructure estimate.
privacy: Local processing. Two external touchpoints to manage: first-run model download from HuggingFace, and the optional remote VLM backends, which send page content to whatever endpoint you configure. Both are controllable; neither is on by default for the standard pipeline.
alternatives: Marker for peak accuracy if the Datalab weights threshold is acceptable
Apache Tika for format breadth without layout
Unstructured as a competing Python-native parser (check its licence tiers)
summary: Document conversion library that parses PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, HTML and images into a unified DoclingDocument model with layout…

name: DocumentCloud
purpose: Hosted and open-source platform for uploading, OCR-ing, searching, annotating and embedding primary-source documents, with an Add-On framework for automation.
journalism_use_case: Where processed documents go to become public evidence: a reporter uploads a 900-page FOIA release, annotates the three paragraphs that matter, and embeds the viewer in the story so readers can read the original. The Add-On model also automates alerts when new documents matching a query appear.
pros: Purpose-built for journalism by a journalism organisation — annotation, embedding and public-document norms are first-class, not adapted from enterprise DMS
The Add-On framework (and Klaxon Cloud as an add-on) lets a newsroom automate monitoring and extraction without running infrastructure
AGPL-3.0 with a real public repository, so the self-hosting option legally exists even if it is not turnkey
Long institutional history (originally IRE/ProPublica lineage, now MuckRock) means the hosted service is unlikely to vanish abruptly
cons: Self-hosting is not a documented turnkey path: Django plus object storage plus a search index, with little deployment documentation — the 54 stars and 56 open issues reflect a repo that exists more for transparency than for third-party operators
The best-performing OCR add-ons are third-party cloud APIs (Google Cloud Vision, Azure Document Intelligence class services), so the accurate path sends your pages to a vendor
The hosted platform stores documents on MuckRock infrastructure under its terms — a third-party custody decision that is unacceptable for unpublished source material in a hostile-state threat model
No GitHub release objects; versioning is informal (latest tag is 'staging-lambda-test'), making a self-hosted deployment hard to pin
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented signals: an active hosted service with public newsroom document collections, against a small code repository (54 stars) with informal tagging. The OCR add-on architecture routing to commercial cloud OCR is documented in the add-on repositories.
assessment: Use the hosted service for documents you have decided to publish; do not use it as your working archive for unpublished material, and do not plan to self-host it unless you are prepared for undocumented Django operations. For your profile the clean division is: OpenAleph or Datashare inside the perimeter for analysis, DocumentCloud at the end for publication and reader-facing embedding. The OCR add-on question has a local answer — OCR with OCRmyPDF before upload rather than using a cloud add-on.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, no release objects, latest tag 'staging-lambda-test', 54 stars, 56 open issues. The hosted service is the primary artefact and is live; the repository is maintained alongside it but is not packaged for external deployment. Active, with the caveat that activity is service-driven rather than release-driven.
model_or_data_licence: n/a for the platform. Cloud OCR add-ons operate under the respective vendor's terms.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0 network copyleft: if you modify DocumentCloud and offer it to users over a network, you must release your modified source. Material if you intend a customised newsroom deployment.
costs: Hosted DocumentCloud access has historically been free to verified journalists with paid organisational tiers; current prices were NOT verified in this survey — treat as not publicly verified here and check with MuckRock. Cloud OCR add-ons incur the underlying vendor's per-page charges (not priced here). Self-hosting costs are Django app servers, object storage and a search index, plus substantial undocumented-deployment engineering effort.
privacy: The hosted service places documents in MuckRock's custody — appropriate for material destined for publication, not for unpublished source documents. Documents can be kept private within the platform, but that is a policy control on someone else's infrastructure, not a technical guarantee under your control. The high-accuracy OCR add-ons send page images to third-party cloud vendors.
alternatives: OpenAleph or ICIJ Datashare for in-perimeter analysis
Uwazi for a public-facing human-rights document collection you host yourself
Paperless-ngx for a modest self-hosted internal archive
blockers: Hosted custody of documents is unsuitable for unpublished sensitive material in a hostile-state threat model
summary: Hosted and open-source platform for uploading, OCR-ing, searching, annotating and embedding primary-source documents…

name: entity-fishing
purpose: Entity recognition and disambiguation service that links text mentions to Wikidata QIDs using an LMDB-backed knowledge base built from Wikidata and Wikipedia dumps, exposed as a REST API.
journalism_use_case: Resolving ambiguous names in a document set to stable identifiers so the same politician spelled three different ways across a leak collapses into one node — the prerequisite for building a reliable entity graph from messy text, and all of it offline.
pros: Fully local entity linking after the knowledge base is built — a genuine and rare advantage over hosted linking APIs when the documents cannot leave your network
Wikidata QIDs are stable, language-independent identifiers, which makes cross-language and cross-dataset joins possible in a way raw NER strings never allow
Multilingual and designed for scale, with a REST interface that drops into any pipeline
Apache-2.0 with the project shipping its own models and knowledge-base builds
cons: Heavy install and a large disk footprint for the LMDB knowledge base — a real operational commitment, not a pip install
The knowledge base goes stale unless you rebuild it from new dumps, and rebuilding is itself a substantial batch job
Coverage is limited to entities that exist in Wikidata, which excludes most shell companies, private individuals and local officials — precisely the entities investigations care about most
No GitHub release objects (latest tag 0.0.6) and 49 open issues against 270 stars; essentially a specialist research tool with a thin community
feedback: No user reports collected. Documented context: same maintainer as GROBID, which has a strong reputation in scholarly document processing — relevant as a credibility signal for engineering quality, not as evidence of newsroom use. No journalism deployment verified.
assessment: Valuable but narrow, and the Wikidata-coverage limit is the decisive constraint for investigative work: it will confidently link the minister and silently miss the shell company. For your profile I would use it where the subject matter is public figures and institutions (political reporting, procurement, academia) and not expect it to help on a corporate-ownership leak. Budget a day for the knowledge-base build and a recurring job to refresh it.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-08-05, latest tag 0.0.6, no release objects, 270 stars, 49 open issues. Commits within the last four months and no deprecation notice, but low velocity and informal versioning. Classified stable-low rather than declining because the maintainer remains active across related projects (GROBID) and the tool is functionally complete.
model_or_data_licence: Ships its own models and knowledge-base builds. The knowledge base derives from Wikidata (CC0) and Wikipedia (CC-BY-SA) — the CC-BY-SA component is worth noting if you redistribute a derived knowledge base.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive. Derived knowledge bases inherit Wikipedia's CC-BY-SA obligations if redistributed.
costs: No fee. Costs are storage (tens of GB for the knowledge base) and a JVM service with several GB of RAM, plus the engineer time to build and periodically rebuild the KB. Infrastructure estimate.
privacy: Fully local once the knowledge base is built; no document text leaves the machine. This is its main argument over cloud entity-linking APIs, which see every document you process.
alternatives: spaCy or GLiNER plus your own gazetteer where targets are known in advance
nomenklatura with FollowTheMoney for entity resolution over structured records
OpenRefine reconciliation against a self-hosted yente instance — but note reconciliation leaks values if pointed at a public service
summary: Entity recognition and disambiguation service that links text mentions to Wikidata QIDs using an LMDB-backed knowledge base built…

name: eScriptorium
maintainer: Scripta / PSL (École Pratique des Hautes Études)
purpose: Web platform for transcribing manuscript and printed images at scale, wrapping Kraken for segmentation and recognition, with collaborative correction, model training and export to ALTO/PAGE XML.
journalism_use_case: Gives a non-engineer team a shared interface over a scanned handwritten archive — colonial-era registers, handwritten ledgers, court records — where reporters' corrections become training data that improves recognition across the remaining thousands of pages. The compounding-accuracy loop is what makes an otherwise impossible archive investigation tractable.
pros: The human-in-the-loop training loop is the real capability: accuracy on a specific hand improves as the team transcribes, rather than being fixed by a generic model
Turns Kraken from an engineer's CLI into something a research team can use collaboratively, with task assignment and review
Exports ALTO and PAGE XML, the standards archives and downstream search tools expect, so the output is not a dead end
Verified active: GitLab API 2026-11-16 last activity, release v26.10 (2026-11-12) — a current project, not a stalled academic prototype
cons: Non-trivial sysadmin burden: Django, PostgreSQL, Redis, Celery workers and GPU scheduling — a bigger operational commitment than any other OCR tool here
Hosted on GitLab, so it is invisible to GitHub-centric discovery and dependency tooling; no GitHub stars to gauge community size (81 GitLab stars)
Throughput is bounded by your own GPU, and HTR training is slow — expect days, not hours, for a usable custom model
Documentation is wiki-based and assumes digital-humanities conventions rather than newsroom workflows
feedback: No user reports collected in this survey. Documented context: eScriptorium is the reference platform in the digital-humanities HTR community and is the standard front end for Kraken, which is a real adoption signal in that adjacent field. No journalism deployment verified — treat newsroom use as unestablished.
assessment: The right tool for a specific and uncommon problem: a large handwritten archive that a team must transcribe together. If your material is typed or printed, Tesseract/OCRmyPDF or Surya will serve you far more cheaply. For media-in-exile work on historical state records this is one of very few viable options, and because it is fully self-hosted it keeps a politically sensitive archive on your own hardware. I would pilot it only with a committed transcription team, since the value depends on sustained human input.
maintenance_evidence: GitLab API 2026-11-17 (project scripta/escriptorium): last_activity_at 2026-11-16, release v26.10 released 2026-11-12, tags v26.10 and v26.10b3 dated 2026-11-05, 81 stars, not archived. Dated releases plus current activity; institutional (PSL/EPHE) backing.
model_or_data_licence: n/a — uses externally supplied Kraken models, whose terms vary per model (Zenodo-published models carry individual licences).
licence_restrictions: Code permissive. Verify the licence of any pretrained Kraken model you import.
costs: No software fee. Real costs: a GPU host for training and inference, a multi-service Django deployment, and — dominantly — human transcription labour to build ground truth. Estimate; assumes self-hosted GPU and a small transcription team.
privacy: Fully self-hosted; images and transcriptions stay on your server with no third-party calls. Appropriate for politically sensitive archives, with the usual caveat that server security and access control are entirely your responsibility.
alternatives: Kraken alone for engineer-driven batch HTR without the collaborative layer
Transkribus for a hosted alternative with a published price list — but it places material with a third party
Surya or PaddleOCR where the material is printed rather than handwritten
summary: Web platform for transcribing manuscript and printed images at scale, wrapping Kraken for segmentation and recognition…

name: eyecite
purpose: Python library that finds, parses and resolves US legal citations in text — full case citations, short forms, supra and id. references — and links them to canonical reporter data.
journalism_use_case: Turns a pile of court filings, briefs or agency decisions into a linked citation graph: which rulings a document relies on, and which other documents in your corpus cite the same case. That is a lead-generation move generic NER cannot make, and it surfaces the brief that quietly depends on a discredited precedent.
pros: Solves a problem no general NLP tool solves — short-form and id. resolution requires domain logic, and eyecite implements it properly
Built and used by Free Law Project behind CourtListener, so it is exercised against millions of real documents rather than a test set
BSD-2-Clause, pure Python, no models to download — trivially auditable and air-gappable
Genuinely complementary: the citation graph is a different axis of analysis from entities or topics
cons: US legal citation formats only — no coverage of other jurisdictions' conventions, which limits it for international investigations
Resolution quality depends on the reporters-db reference dataset; gaps there become gaps in your graph
No GitHub release objects (latest tag v2.7.8), so pinning relies on tags or PyPI rather than release notes
89 open issues against 303 stars; a specialist library with a small community, so edge cases on unusual filings may need your own fixes
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The strongest documented signal is institutional: eyecite is a Free Law Project component used in CourtListener's production citation extraction, which is verifiable from the organisation's repositories. That is credible production evidence at scale within its jurisdiction.
assessment: If you work on US courts, adopt it — there is no alternative of comparable quality, and the citation graph it produces is a distinctive reporting asset. If your work is non-US, it is irrelevant, and I would not try to generalise it. Scored on its intended specialist role: narrow scope is not a defect here, but it does cap journalism-wide relevance.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest tag v2.7.8, no release objects, 303 stars, 89 open issues. Current commits and an active 2.x tag line, backed by a functioning non-profit (Free Law Project) that depends on it operationally.
model_or_data_licence: reporters-db reference data is distributed separately by Free Law Project — check its own terms if you redistribute it.
costs: No fee. Pure CPU, negligible resources. No paid dependencies.
privacy: Entirely local, no network calls, no models — one of the cleanest profiles here. Safe on an air-gapped evidence machine.
alternatives: CourtListener/RECAP for acquiring the filings in the first place
Indigo or laws-africa tooling for non-US legislative documents
Generic NER (spaCy) where citations are not the target
summary: Python library that finds, parses and resolves US legal citations in text — full case citations, short forms, supra and id

name: faster-whisper
purpose: Reimplementation of Whisper inference on CTranslate2, delivering several-fold throughput and memory improvements over the reference implementation, with batched inference and Silero VAD integration.
journalism_use_case: Bulk processing of large audio archives — a press-conference backlog, months of monitored broadcast, a seized recording collection — where throughput per GPU-hour decides whether the investigation is affordable at all.
pros: Throughput and memory profile are the decisive practical advantage: the same GPU budget transcribes several times more audio than reference Whisper
Integrated VAD removes long silences, which both speeds processing and reduces Whisper's well-known tendency to hallucinate text over silence
26,821 stars with only 21 open issues — an exceptionally clean tracker indicating real triage, and the strongest maintenance signal in the transcription subcategory
MIT code and MIT weights, so there is no licence friction for commercial publication
cons: No speaker diarisation — you must add pyannote or WhisperX, and that pulls in HuggingFace gating
The latest release (v1.2.1, 2025-10-31) predates roughly a year of commits, so pinning to a release loses fixes while tracking main loses reproducibility; this is a real operational annoyance
CUDA/cuDNN version mismatches are the standard install failure, and the error messages are unhelpful
Repository was transferred from guillaumekln to SYSTRAN — the old URL redirects, but SBOMs, pinned git URLs and provenance records should be updated to the canonical path
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented signals: 21 open issues against 26.8k stars (strong triage evidence); and the project's own README documents the benchmark claims, which are project claims rather than independently verified measurements. Widely used as the backend of Buzz and WhisperX, verifiable from those projects' dependencies.
assessment: The default engine for any batch transcription work you build, with the caveat that you must decide explicitly between a stale release tag and a moving main branch — I would pin a specific commit and record it in the pipeline's provenance notes. Combine with pyannote for diarisation only if you can accept the HuggingFace gate; otherwise accept unlabelled speakers. Repository transfer verified in this session: guillaumekln/faster-whisper now redirects to SYSTRAN/faster-whisper.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-12, latest release v1.2.1 (2025-10-31), latest tag v1.2.1, 26,821 stars, 21 open issues. The near-empty issue tracker alongside recent commits is the key evidence; the year-old release tag is a release-hygiene gap, not evidence of abandonment.
costs: No fee. Cost is compute: a single mid-range NVIDIA GPU transcribes faster than real time by a wide margin, so a modest on-prem GPU is usually cheaper than per-minute commercial ASR for sustained volume. CPU int8 works for light use. Infrastructure estimate; assumes self-hosted GPU and large-v3-class model.
privacy: Local inference; audio never leaves the machine. The only network event is the first-run weights download from HuggingFace, which can be pre-staged for air-gapped operation.
alternatives: whisper.cpp for CPU-only and field hardware
WhisperX when you need diarisation and word-level alignment
NVIDIA NeMo Speech for peak English accuracy — but check the per-checkpoint licence, some are CC-BY-NC
summary: Reimplementation of Whisper inference on CTranslate2, delivering several-fold throughput and memory improvements over the…

name: FollowTheMoney (alephdata 3.x line)
maintainer: originally OCCRP/Aleph; active development moved to OpenSanctions
purpose: Entity schema and data model for investigative data — Person, Company, Ownership, Payment, Membership and related types — with validation, mapping from tabular sources, and export helpers.
journalism_use_case: The shared vocabulary that makes cross-dataset linking possible: map a leak, a corporate registry and a sanctions list into the same Person/Company/Ownership schema so the records can actually be compared rather than merely co-located. Aleph, OpenAleph, yente and nomenklatura all build on it.
pros: Solves the modelling problem that otherwise blocks every cross-dataset investigation, and does so with a vocabulary designed by investigative practitioners
Ecosystem effect: adopting FtM gives you free interoperability with OpenAleph, yente, nomenklatura and OpenSanctions data
MIT and pure Python — easy to adopt incrementally for a single dataset without buying into a platform
Well-documented schema reference at followthemoney.tech with worked mapping examples
cons: THIS repository is the stale 3.x line: pushed 2026-02-28, latest release v3.8.2 (2025-03-24). Active 4.x development is at opensanctions/followthemoney (v4.11.3, 2026-11-07) and the old URL does NOT redirect — anyone pinning from alephdata is on an abandoned major version
It is an ontology, not a tool: mapping messy real data into it is substantial, unglamorous work that teams consistently underestimate
The schema is opinionated towards financial-crime and corporate investigation; fitting other domains (health records, environmental data) requires compromise
Governance churn across the alephdata/OpenSanctions split is itself a planning risk for a long-lived archive
feedback: No individual user reports. The decisive documented finding from this session's verification: two live repositories exist with the same name and no redirect between them, with a two-major-version gap (3.8.2 versus 4.11.3). That is a concrete dependency trap, verified via the GitHub API on 2026-11-17 and recorded in sources/evidence/leads.md.
assessment: Adopt the model, but from the OpenSanctions repository, not this one. I am cataloguing the alephdata repo separately precisely because it is the URL most documentation and search results still point at, and following it silently puts you on a dead 3.x branch. For your work the ontology is worth the mapping effort if you expect to combine datasets more than once; for a single one-off dataset it is overhead.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-02-28, latest release v3.8.2 (2025-03-24), latest tag v3.8.4, 309 stars, 69 open issues. Nearly nine months without a push and over a year without a release, while the same-named OpenSanctions repository released v4.11.3 on 2026-11-07. Declining rather than archived because no deprecation notice is posted — which is itself the hazard.
costs: No fee. Cost is engineer time writing and maintaining mappings — realistically days per complex source dataset. No paid dependencies.
privacy: Local library only; no network calls, no telemetry.
alternatives: opensanctions/followthemoney — the actively maintained 4.x line, use this instead
nomenklatura and rigour from the same ecosystem for resolution and normalisation
Plain schema design plus Splink if you only ever link two datasets
blockers: This repository is a stale major version with no deprecation notice; development moved to opensanctions/followthemoney and the old URL does not redirect
summary: Entity schema and data model for investigative data — Person, Company, Ownership, Payment, Membership and related types…

name: GLiNER
purpose: Compact bidirectional-transformer NER model that extracts arbitrary user-specified entity types at inference time without retraining, running on CPU or a small GPU.
journalism_use_case: Define bespoke labels for one investigation — 'shell company', 'vessel', 'bank account', 'politically exposed person' — and sweep a leak for them without annotating training data and without sending documents to an API. That flexibility is what spaCy's fixed label set cannot give you.
pros: Zero-shot custom labels change the economics of entity extraction for investigations, where the interesting entity type is always project-specific
Small enough to run on CPU, so it is deployable on an isolated evidence machine rather than requiring GPU infrastructure
Apache-2.0 code with Apache-2.0 v2.1 checkpoints available — a genuinely open path exists
Active development (v0.2.30, 2026-11-02) with a multilingual checkpoint line
cons: Licence trap, verified and material: the older but still widely cited v0/v1 checkpoints (gliner_base, gliner_multi, gliner_small/medium/large-v1) are CC-BY-NC-4.0 and unusable by a commercial newsroom; only the v2.1 line (gliner_small-v2.1, gliner_multi-v2.1) is Apache-2.0
Recall is prompt-sensitive: label wording materially changes what you find, which makes systematic coverage hard to evidence in a methodology note
Long documents must be chunked, and entities spanning chunk boundaries are missed
Extracts but does not link or deduplicate — 'Rosneft Trading' and 'OOO Rosneft-Trading' remain separate strings until you add rigour/nomenklatura
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The documented, checkable finding is the split model licensing recorded in session 1 and retained here: HuggingFace cards for the v0/v1 checkpoints state cc-by-nc-4.0 while the v2.1 cards state apache-2.0. 4,270 stars, 54 open issues.
assessment: High-value and I would use it, but with a hard rule: pin a v2.1 Apache-2.0 checkpoint and record the exact model ID in the pipeline, because the NC checkpoints are the ones most tutorials link to. Treat its output as a candidate list for human review rather than a finding — prompt sensitivity means absence of a hit is not evidence of absence. Pair with rigour for normalisation before any matching.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-11, latest release v0.2.30 (2026-11-02), 4,270 stars, 54 open issues. Frequent releases on a 0.2.x line with current commits; research-origin project that has sustained a release cadence.
model_or_data_licence: SPLIT AND MATERIAL: v2.1 checkpoints (urchade/gliner_small-v2.1, urchade/gliner_multi-v2.1) are Apache-2.0; older v0/v1 checkpoints (urchade/gliner_base, gliner_multi, gliner_small/medium/large-v1) are CC-BY-NC-4.0, research only.
licence_restrictions: Using a v0/v1 checkpoint in commercially published journalism breaches CC-BY-NC-4.0. The code licence does not cure this. Verify the checkpoint, not the repository.
costs: No fee for the Apache-2.0 path. CPU inference is viable; a small GPU speeds bulk sweeps. No paid dependencies. Estimate only.
privacy: Local inference after checkpoint download; no text leaves the machine. Weights can be pre-staged for air-gapped use.
alternatives: spaCy with EntityRuler gazetteers when target names are known in advance
Stanza for non-English NER with conventional label sets

name: GlotLID
purpose: FastText-based language identification model covering over 2,000 language labels with script codes, built to address the low-resource-language gap in standard LID models.
journalism_use_case: Identifies the languages fastText's lid.176 silently misses — minority, diaspora and regional languages in a document dump — so a multilingual leak gets routed to the right translator or MT model instead of being mislabelled as the nearest major language. Because labels carry script codes it distinguishes Serbian in Cyrillic from Serbian in Latin, which matters for sourcing and for choosing a transliteration path.
pros: Coverage of low-resource and minority languages is the whole point and is directly relevant to media-in-exile and diaspora reporting, where major-language LID fails
Script codes in the label set solve a real routing problem that language-only labels cannot
FastText-based: a single model file, millisecond inference on CPU, trivially air-gappable
Licence clarified in this survey — the LICENSE file reads as Apache-2.0 plus notices, not an unknown 'Other'
cons: Thousands of labels mean many confusable low-confidence classes; without a confidence threshold you will get plausible-looking wrong answers on short strings
No tagged releases at all and a research-project cadence, so there is no version to pin other than a commit and a model file hash
The appended notices warn about training-data provenance and model behaviour — a soft caveat that the labels carry research-grade rather than production guarantees
Small community (228 stars, 4 open issues): if it breaks, you are on your own
feedback: No user reports collected. Documented context is academic: GlotLID is published research addressing documented failures of lid.176 on low-resource languages. The tiny issue tracker (4 open) reflects a small user base rather than strong triage.
assessment: Worth adopting as a routing component in any multilingual ingest pipeline, with a confidence floor and a fallback to 'unknown' rather than a forced guess — a mislabelled language quietly corrupts every downstream step. For your profile the low-resource coverage is the specific reason to prefer it over fastText lid.176. Because there are no releases, record the model file's hash alongside your pipeline version so results stay reproducible.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-09, no releases and no tags, 228 stars, 4 open issues. Recent commits but no release engineering; characteristic of a maintained research artefact. Classified stable-low rather than active because there is no release cadence to evidence active maintenance, and not dormant because commits are current.
licence: Apache-2.0 with additional notices (LICENSE file read directly: 'Apache License 2.0 plus notices', with appended notices on training data and model behaviour; GitHub API reports NOASSERTION)
model_or_data_licence: Apache-2.0 with the same additional notices.
licence_restrictions: No field-of-use restriction found. The appended notices are disclaimers about training-data provenance rather than usage limits, but read them before redistributing the model file.
costs: No fee. One model file (hundreds of MB for the full label set), CPU inference, negligible cost.
privacy: Fully local after downloading the model file from HuggingFace; no inference-time network calls.
alternatives: fastText lid.176 where only major languages matter and speed is paramount
